newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe's borrowers look abroad as EMU approaches.
newsitem.headline: Europe's borrowers look abroad as EMU approaches.

text.p: European borrowers are spreading their wings beyond their home markets as European economic and monetary union (EMU) approaches and a desire to cut funding costs forces them to diversify their investor base.

Some of Europe's biggest bond issuers, including names from nations not expected to take part in the first wave of EMU in January 1999, have been raising an increasing proportion of funds in foreign currencies.
And bankers say they expect more borrowers to target foreign investors, particulary when the euro is adopted.
"The creation of this new (euro) market, of similar size to the U.S., will create opportunities for all kinds of new borrowers," said David Tory, head of debt syndication at Merrill Lynch in London.
Norddeutsche Landesbank underlined a dilemma facing German borrowers in particular when it announced its first guilder bond issue last month.

Management board member Juergen Koesters said he expected that once the euro was introduced, foreign borrowers previously put off by currency risk would be competing against German issuers to sell bonds to German investors.

He said Nord LB, which has issued its first French franc and peseta bonds in the last 18 months, was strengthening its funding in other European currencies as part of an investor relations campaign ahead of EMU.
"We are losing the advantage of the deutschemark. That means we have to go, look around and make ourselves well known," he told a news conference.

BNG, a AAA-rated Dutch local authorities bank, recently went on a roadshow in Asia and it plans to build up recognition of its name among European institutional investors in a bid to broaden its investor base.

BNG, the biggest Dutch issuer in international capital markets, in 1996 raised 65 percent of its borrowings in European currencies which it expects to participate in EMU. Before 1993, BNG issued only in guilders.

Senior vice-president Treasury Bert de Kock conceded this strategy took account of the approach of EMU, saying BNG would be a big borrower in euros. "We want to attract investors outside and in Europe," he said.
Dutch Co-operative Rabobank raised more than half of its capital markets borrowings in foreign currencies in 1996, compared with none at the start of this decade.
Rabobank International's head of funding and structures, Theo Hendriks, said the bank was looking to tap new markets, having issued in more than 10 foreign currencies since 1991.
British bank Abbey National, the biggest British issuer of international bonds in the first half of 1997, said it expected to raise more funds from European investors after EMU.

"In France, where investors started to diversify away from French names, we have become one of the largest borrowers in the French franc Eurobond market. Hopefully that will spill over into other currencies," said Alex Braun, director at Abbey National Treasury Services.

Italy's biggest capital markets issuer this year, the Italian state, has launched French franc, guilder, ecu and mark bonds this year which redenominate in euros, and in March became the first sovereign borrower to raise funds in euros.
But EMU would also be favourable for non-governmental issuers, allowing them to access a broader investor base, said David Munves, Eurobond strategist at Lehman Brothers.

"Right now many European institutional investors have to buy assets denominated in their home currency. After the introduction of the euro, they will have much more choice in what credits they buy within the euro block," Munves said.
One syndication manager said European borrowers were interested in raising their profiles among institutional investors throughout the different EMU currencies.
"The only problem is matching institutional demand with the funding targets of different borrowers," he said.
Spanish borrowers also have been diversifying the currencies in which they borrow, particularly over the last four to five years, seeking lower funding costs.
"This is due to the fact they are always looking for the best bargain. This is true especially for the (Spanish) Treasury," said one syndicate manager in Spain.
